meta_story.title: The Contested Republic
meta_story.tagline: Who claimed liberty and who wielded power
meta_story.description:
American independence emerged from more than battlefield victories. It was fought through military campaigns and frontier alliances, carried across the Atlantic by diplomats, argued in pamphlets and private letters, and tested by the difficult work of designing a government capable of surviving peace. The struggle joined people with sharply different commitments and experiences, including Patriot leaders, an enslaved poet asserting authorship and liberty, and a Mohawk leader defending his people’s political future through a British alliance.

From resistance to imperial rule through the presidencies of the new republic, public action took many forms. Washington commanded an army; Franklin secured indispensable French support; Jefferson gave independence its most famous language; Hamilton built federal finance; and Adams, Warren, and Wheatley made political life visible in correspondence, satire, and verse. Brant’s campaigns and diplomacy reveal that the Revolution was also a devastating contest over Indigenous homelands, sovereignty, and the boundaries of the expanding United States.

hints.hint: Focus on the struggle for independence and the contested work of building the early United States; balance military command, diplomacy, political advocacy, correspondence, constitutional design, and public finance.

chapters.title: Arguments Against Empire (1729-1775)

person_events.theme_connection: Benjamin Franklin and Hugh Meredith bought The Pennsylvania Gazette from printer Samuel Keimer. Franklin used the Philadelphia newspaper for news, satire, essays, and arguments for local reform.
Franklin told the House of Commons that the colonies opposed the Stamp Act, which taxed legal documents, newspapers, and other printed material. Parliament repealed the law on March 18, 1766.

person_events.event_title: Her First Poem Appears in Print
person_events.theme_connection: At about fourteen, Phillis Wheatley saw her elegy for two men lost at sea printed in Newport. The publication introduced an enslaved Black girl to colonial readers as a poet.

Mercy Otis Warren anonymously published The Adulateur, a satirical play attacking Massachusetts Governor Thomas Hutchinson. Its character Brutus represented her brother James Otis Jr. and the Patriot cause.

After Boston publishers declined her manuscript, Wheatley published Poems on Various Subjects, Religious and Moral in London with support from the Countess of Huntingdon. The volume included an attestation from Boston leaders who said Wheatley had written the poems.

While studying at King’s College, Alexander Hamilton anonymously published A Full Vindication of the Measures of Congress and The Farmer Refuted. The pamphlets answered Loyalist minister Samuel Seabury and defended resistance to British rule.

Joseph Brant traveled from Montreal to London with British official Guy Johnson as war spread through New York. Brant met King George III and colonial secretary George Germain while seeking British support for Mohawk interests.
Warren anonymously published The Group as fighting began. The satire imagined a king canceling the Massachusetts charter and attacked officials who supported royal authority.

historical_context.title: Coercive Acts
historical_context.description: Britain's Parliament passed punitive laws in 1774 that closed Boston's port and curtailed Massachusetts self-government after the Boston Tea Party. The measures drew Washington into the First Continental Congress and intensified the Massachusetts resistance that Mercy Otis Warren championed in print.

chapters.lead_in: Printers, poets, playwrights, and pamphleteers carried resistance into public life. Their appeals also exposed competing claims to liberty within the British Empire.

chapters.title: Independence at War (1776-1783)

person_events.theme_connection: Writing from Braintree to John Adams in Philadelphia, Abigail Adams urged lawmakers to “remember the ladies” when creating new laws. She warned against giving husbands unlimited legal power.

Franklin served with Thomas Jefferson, John Adams, Roger Sherman, and Robert Livingston on the committee that prepared the Declaration of Independence. The Continental Congress revised the committee’s text before adopting it.

George Washington led Continental soldiers across the ice-filled Delaware River and attacked the Hessian garrison at Trenton. The Americans captured the garrison and recovered their position in New Jersey.
Thomas Jefferson drafted the Declaration of Independence for the five-member committee in Philadelphia. The Continental Congress revised his text and adopted it on July 4, 1776.

Joseph Brant led about 400 Mohawk and other Indigenous allies with British rangers in an ambush near Oriska, New York. They attacked Patriot militia and Oneida warriors advancing to relieve Fort Stanwix.
Franklin, Arthur Lee, and Silas Deane signed two treaties with France in Paris. One established trade, while the other committed France to military cooperation against Britain.

American and French forces under Washington and the Comte de Rochambeau surrounded the British army at Yorktown. French warships under the Comte de Grasse blocked the British escape through Chesapeake Bay.
Franklin signed the Treaty of Paris with John Adams and John Jay. Britain recognized the independence of the United States and formally ended the Revolutionary War.
Washington resigned as commander in chief before the Continental Congress in Annapolis. He returned military authority to civilian representatives and went home to Mount Vernon.

historical_context.title: Valley Forge
historical_context.description: Washington's Continental Army encamped through the winter of 1777–78 at Valley Forge, Pennsylvania, suffering severe shortages, disease, and cold while undergoing training. Washington commanded the struggling army there, and Hamilton served beside him as an aide-de-camp handling crucial military correspondence and administration.

historical_context.title: Sullivan Expedition
historical_context.description: Continental forces under John Sullivan invaded Haudenosaunee territory in 1779, burning villages and food stores in an effort to destroy Indigenous nations allied with Britain. The campaign displaced Iroquois communities and intensified the frontier war in which Joseph Brant commanded Mohawk and other British-allied forces.

chapters.lead_in: Declarations and letters defined the cause while armies fought over its survival. Indigenous alliances and European intervention widened the conflict beyond a war between Britain and its colonies.

chapters.title: Terms of the Republic (1784-1790)

person_events.theme_connection: A proclamation by Governor Frederick Haldimand granted Mohawks and other Haudenosaunee allies land along the Grand River in present-day Ontario. Brant led families there from former settlements in New York.
Brant returned to London on behalf of the Grand River Haudenosaunee communities. He pressed British ministers for secure title to their land and compensation for wartime losses.
Hamilton began writing The Federalist with James Madison and John Jay under the shared name Publius. Their essays answered objections to the proposed Constitution during the ratification campaign.
Delegates elected Washington to preside over the Constitutional Convention in Philadelphia. They had gathered to revise the Articles of Confederation and produced a new Constitution.
Warren published Observations on the New Constitution under the name A Columbian Patriot. She opposed ratification and called for a Bill of Rights to protect individual liberties.

As treasury secretary, Hamilton submitted the Report on Public Credit to Congress. He proposed federal repayment of the national debt and federal assumption of state war debts, drawing opposition from James Madison and Thomas Jefferson.

historical_context.title: Fort Stanwix Treaty
historical_context.description: United States commissioners secured a 1784 treaty from several Iroquois representatives that demanded vast land cessions after the war. Joseph Brant rejected its treatment of Haudenosaunee sovereignty, and the loss of recognized territory strengthened his efforts to secure Mohawk land and political backing at Grand River and in London.

historical_context.title: Shays' Rebellion
historical_context.description: Indebted Massachusetts farmers led by Daniel Shays forcibly closed courts and attempted to seize a federal arsenal before state militia forces dispersed them. The uprising alarmed Washington and Hamilton and supplied a powerful practical case for the stronger federal system they pursued.

chapters.lead_in: Peace left debts, displaced communities, and a weak national government. Constitutional debate turned revolutionary allies into opponents over the distribution of political power.

chapters.title: Power in Practice (1796-1805)

person_events.theme_connection: Near the end of his second presidential term, Washington published his Farewell Address in Philadelphia and announced that he would not seek a third term. He revised an earlier draft by James Madison with help from Hamilton.

Hamilton published a detailed account of his affair with Maria Reynolds after accusations that his payments to her husband involved public corruption. The Reynolds Pamphlet placed his private conduct before a national political audience.

American envoys Robert Livingston and James Monroe signed the Louisiana Purchase agreement with France in Paris. Acting under Jefferson’s instructions, they acquired New Orleans and the Louisiana territory for $15 million.

Warren published her three-volume History of the Rise, Progress, and Termination of the American Revolution. Illness, periods of blindness, and the deaths of three sons had delayed the work, and Jefferson ordered copies for himself and his cabinet.

historical_context.title: Haitian Revolution
historical_context.description: Enslaved people in the French colony of Saint-Domingue began a revolution in 1791 and defeated French forces, creating independent Haiti in 1804. France's failure to restore its Caribbean colony helped induce Napoleon to sell Louisiana, enabling Jefferson's purchase and transforming the scale of the republic he governed.

chapters.lead_in: National authority soon operated through public finance, partisan print, diplomacy, and territorial expansion. Political leaders also began writing their own accounts of the republic and its origins.

conclusion.text: John Adams declined Abigail Adams’s proposed “extraordinary code of laws.” The republic widened far beyond the colonies and placed greater authority in a federal government. Women remained outside formal political power, slavery endured, and Haudenosaunee communities faced displacement. The request from Braintree remained unanswered by the political settlement these connected lives made and contested.

circles.title: Letters and Encouragement
circles.text: Abigail Adams and Mercy Otis Warren were close friends and regular correspondents. Adams encouraged Warren to continue writing political satire when Warren doubted whether the work suited a woman. Their letters gave both writers a place to discuss public affairs beyond formal institutions that excluded them.

circles.title: Around Washington
circles.text: Franklin joined the Constitutional Convention that Washington presided over, and he had previously worked with Jefferson on the Declaration of Independence. Hamilton served on Washington’s wartime staff and later joined Jefferson in Washington’s cabinet, where the two secretaries became political opponents. Wheatley sent Washington a poem, received his praise, and gained an invitation to his military headquarters. Jefferson later dismissed the value of Wheatley’s poetry. Brant met Washington after fighting on the British side and defending Haudenosaunee communities targeted by the Sullivan Expedition that Washington ordered.

stops.title: Making National Government
stops.text: Philadelphia joined print culture to national government. Franklin acquired The Pennsylvania Gazette there, and Franklin and Jefferson worked there on the Declaration of Independence. Washington later presided over the Constitutional Convention, Hamilton submitted his public credit plan, and Washington published his Farewell Address in the city.

stops.title: Appeals to Imperial Power
stops.text: London held Parliament, the royal court, and publishers who could reach readers across the empire. Franklin testified there against the Stamp Act, and Wheatley found a publisher there for her poetry. Brant visited twice to seek British support for Mohawk land and political claims.

stops.title: Diplomacy in Paris
stops.text: Paris supplied the alliances and agreements that altered the republic’s position in the world. Franklin signed the French alliance treaties there during the war and the peace treaty recognizing independence afterward. American envoys returned to the French capital to complete the Louisiana Purchase under Jefferson.

stops.title: The Chesapeake Trap
stops.text: Yorktown stood beside waterways that allowed French naval power to shape the siege. French ships blocked Chesapeake Bay while American and French troops surrounded the British army. The British surrender ended the war’s decisive campaign.

stops.title: Returning Military Power
stops.text: The Continental Congress was meeting in the Maryland State House at Annapolis when Washington resigned his commission. He surrendered command to civilian representatives after the war and returned to Mount Vernon.

opening.text: On March 31, 1776, Abigail Adams sat in Braintree, Massachusetts, and wrote to her husband in Philadelphia. John Adams was serving in the Continental Congress as delegates considered independence and new governments. She urged him to “remember the ladies” when lawmakers drafted new laws. She warned against giving husbands unlimited legal power.

image.caption: Abigail Adams letter concerning women's rights

description.text: Adams’s warning placed women’s legal status inside the coming struggle over republican government. The American Revolution began as colonial resistance to laws imposed by Britain and developed into a war for independence. A republic locates political authority in the people and their representatives. Political rights in the colonies were narrowly held, slavery was legal, and Indigenous nations defended their own sovereignty. Independence ended royal rule without settling who belonged within the new political order. The Constitution later strengthened the federal government as arguments over rights, debt, and representation continued. By 1805, the United States had survived war, formed opposing parties, and expanded through the Louisiana Purchase. The boundaries of its declared liberty remained disputed.

timeline.text: Parliament’s Coercive Acts closed Boston’s port and restricted self-government in Massachusetts, pushing colonial resistance toward war. Printed arguments first gave that resistance a public language. War then made military survival and foreign aid urgent. The peace settlement left displaced Indigenous communities, wartime debts, and a national government with limited powers under the Articles of Confederation. Economic unrest increased support for a stronger federal system. The sequence moves from opposition to independence, then from constitutional design to the daily use of national power. Each stage opened disputes that the previous stage had left unresolved.

network.text: Political society in the revolutionary era was small enough for writers, officers, diplomats, and officeholders to meet repeatedly. Letters carried private advice and political criticism across long distances. Newspapers and pamphlets turned personal arguments into public disputes. Congress, military headquarters, diplomatic missions, and the first presidential cabinet brought collaborators into sustained contact. Friendship could support authorship or secure access to power. War and party conflict could turn acquaintance into opposition. The relationships form clusters around correspondence and national leadership, with a few people linking circles that otherwise occupied different positions in the struggle.

map.text: Political work gathered where institutions could give decisions force. Colonial presses and the Continental Congress drew arguments into major cities. Parliament and the royal court made Britain essential to petitions from across the empire. The French government offered the money, military support, and treaty negotiations needed by the United States. Battlefields acquired their importance from roads, rivers, ports, and naval access. Statehouses provided settings where military authority could return to civilian representatives. The resulting geography stretches across the Atlantic, while a small number of cities repeatedly concentrate writing, negotiation, and government.

composition.throughline: The American Revolution created a republic through print, war, diplomacy, and constitutional argument. The people connected to that work also exposed its disputed boundaries, including women’s legal status, Black authorship, Indigenous sovereignty, federal power, and territorial expansion.
